BG:B001323.description: Nicholas Joseph Begich Sr. was an American politician, school counselor, and school administrator. He served in the Alaska state senate for eight years before being elected in 1970 as a member of the United States House of Representatives from Alaska. He is presumed to have died in the crash of a light aircraft in Alaska in October 1972; his body was never found. He was a member of the Democratic Party.

BG:A000055.description: Robert Brown Aderholt is an American politician and attorney from Alabama. A socially conservative member of the Republican Party and a member of the Tea Party Caucus, he is currently serving as a U.S. representative, representing Alabama's 4th congressional district since 1997. The district includes most of Tuscaloosa County north of the Black Warrior River, as well as Birmingham's far northern suburbs in Walker County and the southern suburbs of Huntsville and Decatur.

BG:W000809.description: Stephen Allen Womack is an American politician serving as the U.S. representative for Arkansas's 3rd congressional district since 2011. The district covers much of northwestern Arkansas, including Fort Smith, Fayetteville, Springdale, and Womack's hometown of Rogers. Before he was elected to Congress, Womack was mayor of Rogers. He is a member of the Republican Party.

The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds for Ukraine Security Assistance, except for U.S. embassy security.

The House voted on a motion to recommit the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2027, which failed, allowing the bill to proceed.
The House rejected an amendment to prohibit the use of $2.1 billion in appropriated funds for Jordan, including military and health programs.
The Amendment sought to prohibit funds appropriated by the Act from being used for Israel, and accordingly reduces the Foreign Military Financing Program account by $3,300,000,000.

Passed the Ukraine Support Act to provide military and financial assistance to Ukraine.

The resolution would have directed the removal of U.S. armed forces from Venezuela that have not been authorized by Congress.
The House failed to adopt a concurrent resolution directing the removal of U.S. armed forces from unauthorized hostilities in or against Venezuela.

The House voted down an amendment that would have struck funding for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative from the appropriations bill.

The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds from the bill for assistance to Ukraine.
The House voted down an amendment to strike funding for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization Security Investment Program.
The House passed the Israel Security Assistance Support Act, providing security assistance to Israel.

House voted on a motion to recommit the Israel Security Assistance Support Act, which would have sent the bill back to committee with instructions to add conditions on aid to Israel; the motion failed.
The House passed a supplemental appropriations bill providing military and security aid to Israel.

Passed the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, providing emergency funding for military assistance, including the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative and Foreign Military Financing, as well as economic support and refugee assistance.

The House voted on a motion to recommit the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, which would have provided military and security assistance to Ukraine, and the motion failed, allowing the bill to proceed.
The House voted down an amendment to eliminate all non-military funding for Ukraine from the supplemental appropriations bill.
The House passed H.R. 6323, the Iran Counterterrorism Act, imposing new sanctions on Iran.

The House passed a bill to rescind presidential waivers and licenses that allowed for the transfer of approximately $6 billion in blocked Iranian funds, effectively reinstating sanctions restrictions on those assets.

The bill restricts the President's authority to unilaterally terminate or waive Iran sanctions, and requires the President to report to Congress before taking such actions. Congress has 30 days (extendable to 60 days) to review the report, and can enact a joint resolution approving or disapproving the action. If Congress disapproves, the President is prohibited from taking the action. The bill als
The bill would impose sanctions on Ansarallah and foreign persons associated with them, and designate them as a foreign terrorist organization.

The bill eliminates a sunset clause in the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996, making permanent the requirement for the President to impose sanctions on certain individuals or entities engaged in specified transactions related to Iran's energy sector or Iran's efforts to acquire or develop certain weapons (such as chemical, biological, or nuclear weapons). The bill passed.

The bill passed the House of Representatives on April 16, 2024, imposing sanctions on Iran for its support of acts of international terrorism, proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and providing financial assistance to Iran.
The bill requires the President to report on funds held by certain Iranian leaders and mandates U.S. and foreign financial institutions to close those accounts, imposing sanctions on Iranian leaders.

Passed the No U.S. Financing for Iran Act, which prohibits U.S. financial institutions from transacting with Iran and bars U.S. support for IMF financial assistance to Iran, with exceptions for humanitarian goods.

Passed the Iran-China Energy Sanctions Act, which imposes secondary sanctions on Chinese financial institutions that purchase petroleum from Iran by barring U.S. financial institutions from maintaining accounts with them.

Passed the Upholding the Dayton Peace Agreement Through Sanctions Act, which imposes visa and property-blocking sanctions on foreign persons threatening the peace, stability, or territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The bill would provide supplemental security assistance to Israel; a 'Nay' vote opposes the aid.

The House passed the No Funds for Iranian Terrorism Act, which requires the President to impose property-blocking sanctions on foreign financial institutions that facilitate transactions involving specific Iranian funds transferred to Qatar.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the President from exercising waiver authority regarding sanctions on Iran under the 2012 NDAA and the Iran Freedom and Counter-Proliferation Act.
The House agreed to an amendment to H.R. 5961 prohibiting the use of federal funds to make funds available to Iran.

Passed the Hamas and Other Palestinian Terrorist Groups International Financing Prevention Act, which imposes mandatory property-blocking sanctions and bars foreign governments supporting designated terrorist groups from receiving U.S. assistance and exports.
Amendment to prohibit using funds to transfer cluster munitions to any foreign country.
The vote was on an amendment to prohibit funds from being made available to Pakistan under H.R. 4665.
The Amendment failed to prohibit funds from being used to provide assistance to Iraq.
The amendment prohibits the use of funds for the Lebanese Armed Forces.
The amendment prohibits the use of funds to initiate a drawdown and delivery of defense articles and services from Department of Defense stocks to Ukraine.
The House failed to approve an amendment to prohibit assistance to Ukraine.
The amendment sought to prohibit Department of Defense funds from being used to transfer cluster munitions to foreign countries.
The amendment sought to prohibit all security assistance for Ukraine under the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2024.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce funding for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative by $300 million.
The House voted down an amendment to reduce the NATO Security Investment Program account by $73.3 million.
Amendment to cut $3 million from the NATO Security Investment Program and apply the savings to the Spending Reduction Account.
The amendment to H.R. 2670 prohibits sanctions relief for the Taliban unless explicitly authorized by Congress, effectively tightening the existing sanctions regime.
The House voted down an amendment that would have struck Section 217 of the NDAA, which authorizes funding for the NATO Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) initiative.
The House rejected an amendment that would have prohibited the sale or transfer of cluster munitions to Ukraine.
The House voted down an amendment that would have struck a provision funding a feasibility study for a U.S. Center of Excellence in Ukraine.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited providing security assistance to Ukraine.
The House voted on a resolution directing the President to remove U.S. armed forces from Somalia under the War Powers Resolution, which failed.
The House voted on a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from Syria pursuant to the War Powers Resolution.

The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the sale of new F-16s or upgrade technology to Turkey unless the President certifies that the transfer is in the U.S. national interest and includes steps to prevent unauthorized overflights of Greece.
The House voted down an amendment to prohibit U.S. military presence in Syria without congressional approval within one year.

Passed the Isolate Russian Government Officials Act of 2022, requiring U.S. agencies to exclude Russian government officials from international financial meetings and forums until Russia ceases destabilizing activities in Ukraine.
Passed the Russia and Belarus Financial Sanctions Act of 2022, requiring U.S. financial institutions to ensure their foreign subsidiaries comply with U.S. sanctions on Russia and Belarus.

Passed the Additional Ukraine Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2022, providing $40.1 billion in emergency aid including defense equipment, economic assistance, and refugee support to Ukraine in response to Russia's invasion.

Passed the Stop Iranian Drones Act, which expands sanctions to cover the provision of unmanned combat aerial vehicles to Iran and requires the designation of Iranian entities that attack U.S. citizens with drones as foreign terrorist organizations.

Passed the Asset Seizure for Ukraine Reconstruction Act, which establishes a working group to determine legal mechanisms for seizing assets of Russian officials and recommends additional energy-related sanctions on Russia.
The House voted to suspend normal trade relations with Russia and Belarus and authorize additional visa and property-blocking sanctions in response to the war in Ukraine.
Passed a bill suspending normal trade relations with Russia and Belarus and authorizing the President to impose increased tariffs and permanent human rights sanctions.
The bill bans the importation of Russian energy products, imposing trade sanctions on Russia.
The House agreed to an amendment requiring the suspension of U.S. sustainment and maintenance support to Saudi Air Force units responsible for civilian casualties in Yemen.
The amendment terminated U.S. military logistical support, spare parts transfers, and coordination efforts for Saudi and UAE-led coalition forces conducting strikes in Yemen.
The amendment to prohibit U.S. military presence in Syria without Congressional approval within one year of enactment failed.
Passed the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act for FY2022, which included funding for foreign aid, military assistance, and international organizations.
House voted to repeal the Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002.
The House voted 204-2 to reject a motion to repeal the Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002.

BG:A000381.tier_writeup: Yassamin Ansari is a sitting Democrat from Arizona who has shown strong anti-interventionist tendencies on the use of force and war authorizations, voting against her party on several occasions to repeal AUMFs and direct the removal of troops. However, her record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is mixed, with an initial interventionist vote in July 2025 followed by an anti-interventionist vote in July 2026, failing the consistency test required for reliability. While she has broken with her party on specific war powers resolutions, she has voted with her party on major military aid packages for Ukraine and Taiwan, indicating a selective rather than principled anti-interventionist stance. Her lack of consistent opposition to military aid to other countries and her inconsistent record on Israel prevent her from being classified as a hard ally. The record shows a member who is moving in an anti-interventionist direction but has not yet established the reliability needed to be counted on when votes get hard.
BG:A000381.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because her record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent and she has not demonstrated the required consistency on the other four areas of interventionism.

BG:G000606.tier_writeup: Adelita Grijalva is a sitting Democrat in Arizona's 7th district who has demonstrated a strong anti-interventionist stance on the use of force, voting consistently against unauthorized hostilities in Iran, Venezuela, and Lebanon. Her record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is clean, with a single anti-interventionist vote that broke with her party, and she has cosponsored the Block the Bombs Act. However, her record fails the reliability test in the military aid area, where she voted in favor of the Ukraine Support Act and sanctions on Taiwan, aligning with her party's interventionist positions. While she signed multiple discharge petitions, these were largely aligned with her party's majority rather than breaking with leadership on specific interventionist measures. The combination of principled anti-war votes on force and consistent interventionist votes on military aid to other countries creates a mixed record that does not meet the threshold for a reliable ally. She is likely to hold her anti-war positions on force but cannot be counted on to oppose military aid to other nations.
BG:G000606.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because she voted for military aid to Ukraine and Taiwan, failing the anti-interventionist test in the military aid area despite strong anti-war votes.

BG:B001287.tier_writeup: Representative Ami Bera is a sitting House Democrat from California who is retiring. Across 71 focus votes, Bera voted anti-interventionist only 23 times (a 32 percent anti ratio), with 22 of those votes matching the majority of his own party. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, his record is inconsistent, having voted for military assistance in H.R. 8034 on April 20, 2024, and voting against amendments to reduce Israeli funding on July 18, 2025. His record on military aid to other countries is similarly interventionist, consistently supporting military assistance to Ukraine and Taiwan while opposing funding restrictions. While Bera has built a consistent record on war authorizations and recently supported resolutions directing the removal of U.S. forces under the War Powers Resolution, these votes coincided with Democratic party majorities rather than principled defections against leadership. With only one breaking anti-interventionist vote recorded and zero discharge petitions signed against his own party leadership, Bera demonstrates partisan alignment rather than anti-establishment independence. TrackAIPAC lists no tracked contributions for Bera in the provided data, but his overall record shows he cannot be counted on when a hard anti-interventionist vote cuts against party line.
BG:B001287.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because his anti-intervention record is inconsistent, heavily reliant on party-line votes, and fails to show sustained defiance of establishment leadership or consistency on core foreign aid measures.

BG:H001090.tier_writeup: Josh Harder (D-CA-9) has served since 2019 and sits on the Appropriations Committee. His anchor-area record on aid to Israel is inconsistent: three anti votes (Feb 2024, May 2024, Jul 2026) and three interventionist votes (Apr 2024, May 2024 motion to recommit, Jul 2025), with no clean turn-and-hold pattern. On military aid to other countries he is largely interventionist (3 of 31 anti), though consistent against aid to Saudi Arabia and Turkey. He votes anti on use of force abroad (9 of 15) and war authorizations (5 of 5), but 19 of his 20 anti votes align with his party majority; only one breaking anti vote exists overall, and zero discharge petitions against his own leadership. No tracked Israel-lobby money appears, but his anti votes cluster with Democratic leadership, suggesting partisanship rather than principle. He falls short of the floor for a sitting member: no sustained anchor consistency and insufficient own-party defections.
BG:H001090.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because his record on aid to Israel is inconsistent and he lacks sufficient own-party defections to demonstrate principle over partisanship.

Under pressure from party leadership he is likely to revert to the Democratic line, making him an unreliable ally.

BG:M001225.tier_writeup: Kevin Mullin is a sitting Democrat from California who has served in Congress since 2023. His record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent, with only 3 of 6 votes being anti-interventionist, including a Yea vote on supplemental security assistance in 2024 and a Nay on an amendment to prohibit funds for Israeli Cooperative Security in 2025. He has voted consistently interventionist on military aid to other countries, voting Nay on amendments to prohibit funding for Ukraine, Lebanon, and Taiwan, and Yea on the PROTECT Taiwan Act and Ukraine Support Act. While he has voted anti-interventionist on war authorizations and some use of force resolutions, these votes largely align with his party's majority position rather than representing a principled break. Mullin received approximately $600,000 in support from AIPAC during his 2022 primary, indicating strong ties to the Israel lobby. His voting record lacks the consistency and independent principle required to be considered a reliable anti-establishment ally, as he frequently votes with his party on interventionist measures.
BG:M001225.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because his record shows consistent interventionist voting on military aid to other countries and inconsistent, often pro-Israel aid votes, despite some anti-war authorization votes that align with his party.

BG:K000389.tier_writeup: Ro Khanna (D-CA17) has a mixed record across the five anti-interventionist areas. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, he has voted anti-interventionist three of four times but broke in July 2025 to vote against an amendment striking funding for Israeli cooperative programs, then returned to an anti vote in July 2026, showing inconsistency rather than a principled turn. Military aid to other countries is similarly inconsistent: he votes reliably against arms for Saudi Arabia and Turkey but has supported aid packages for Ukraine and Taiwan in 2025-2026. Sanctions and use-of-force votes have become consistently anti-interventionist in recent congresses, and he has voted against all five war authorization measures. He has nine party defections on anti-interventionist votes, but most of his anti votes align with his party majority, and he has not signed any discharge petitions that circumvent his own leadership. No Israel-lobby or war-profiteer money is tracked. The record shows genuine anti-war impulses but lacks the anchor consistency and leadership defiance required for reliability.
BG:K000389.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he is inconsistent on the anchor issue of aid to Israel and on military aid to other countries.

BG:C001112.tier_writeup: Salud Carbajal is a sitting Democratic member of the U.S. House representing California's 24th district. His record shows mixed anti-interventionist behavior: he has voted anti on several war‑authorizations and some use‑of‑force resolutions, and he signed multiple discharge petitions that bypass his party's leadership, indicating some principled defiance. However, his votes on aid to Israel are inconsistent—he has cast both pro‑ and anti‑Israel aid votes, failing the anchor requirement of never or consistently never supporting Israel aid. His military aid votes to other countries are also inconsistent, and while he has become more consistent on sanctions and use‑of‑force measures, the lack of consistent anti‑Israel voting disqualifies him as a reliable anti‑establishment ally.
BG:C001112.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because anti-intervention votes are inconsistent with pro-Israel aid votes and statements, and no consistent anti-establishment signal on the anchor issue.

BG:B001285.tier_writeup: Julia Brownley (D-CA-26) is a sitting House member who is retiring after the 2026 primary. Her record on the anchor issue — aid to the State of Israel — is inconsistent: three anti votes and three interventionist votes across six roll calls, with no sustained turn against aid. She has only two breaking anti-intervention votes in total, one on Israel aid (2024-02-06) and one on cluster munitions (2023-09-28), and zero votes defecting from her own party leadership on discharge petitions or other procedural fights. Of her 24 anti-intervention focus votes, 22 were cast with the Democratic majority, indicating partisanship rather than principle. On military aid to other countries she is inconsistent (4 of 32 anti), recently voting for Taiwan and Ukraine assistance. Sanctions and use-of-force votes became consistent only later, and war-authorization votes are consistently anti but always with her party. No TrackAIPAC money is recorded, but she has also not been targeted by pro-Israel spending. The record falls below the floor for a sitting member: no sustained anchor consistency, no leadership defiance, and anti votes that track party lines.
BG:B001285.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because she is inconsistent on the anchor issue of aid to Israel, has only two breaking votes total with zero defections against her own leadership, and 22 of 24 anti-intervention votes align with the Democratic majority.

BG:R000620.tier_writeup: Luz Rivas (D-CA-29) has served in the House since 2025. Her record on the anchor issue — aid to Israel — is interventionist: she voted NAY on two amendments to restrict Israeli cooperative programs (HR 4016, July 2025; HR 8595, July 2026) and cosponsored the United States-Israel Defense Partnership Act of 2025 (HR 1229). She has zero breaking anti-interventionist votes on Israel aid. On supporting areas, she votes anti on use-of-force and war-authorization measures but almost always with her party majority (97–100% same); her only notable party defection is a YEA on H CON RES 84 (Lebanon withdrawal, June 2026) where only 43% of Democrats agreed. She has signed no discharge petitions that defy her own leadership. She also cosponsored the Enhanced Iran Sanctions Act (HR 1422) and the PROTECT Taiwan Act (HR 1531) and Ukraine Support Act (HR 2913), all interventionist military-aid bills. TrackAIPAC records show no direct contributions, but press reports confirm she joined an AIPAC-funded congressional trip to Israel in August 2025. Her first anti vote came nine months into her term, and she has not held a consistent anti line on the anchor issue. The pattern is partisan alignment, not principled anti-interventionism.
BG:R000620.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because Luz Rivas has voted interventionist on aid to Israel (the anchor issue) and has no breaking anti-interventionist votes on that issue, while cosponsoring pro-Israel legislation.

Outside spending, including from the United Democracy Project, and a narrow primary margin create political and capital risks that further undermine his reliability as an anti‑establishment ally.

BG:K000400.tier_writeup: Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-CA-37) has served in the House since 2023. Her record on the anchor issue — aid to Israel — is inconsistent: she voted against two Israel aid measures in 2024 (HR 7217, HR 8369) but voted for the $14.3 billion Israel Security Supplemental (HR 8034) and against an amendment to strike Israeli cooperative funding (HR 4016) in 2025, then voted for an anti-aid amendment in 2026 (HR 8595). This flip-flopping fails the requirement that a sitting member vote anti-interventionist on Israel aid and stay consistent. On military aid to other countries she is also inconsistent (5 of 29 anti), voting against cluster munitions amendments but for major Ukraine, Taiwan, and Lebanon aid packages. She has become consistent on sanctions (6 of 12 anti), use of force abroad (9 of 12 anti), and war authorizations (3 of 3 anti), but many of those anti votes came with her party majority. She has 8 breaking anti votes against her party, yet she has not signed any discharge petitions that defy her own leadership (all petitions she signed had 100% Democratic signers). No AIPAC or war-profiteer money is tracked, but the anchor inconsistency and lack of own-leadership defiance mean she cannot be counted as reliable.
BG:K000400.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because she has voted inconsistently on aid to Israel, including voting for a major Israel military aid package in 2024, and has not signed discharge petitions against her own leadership.

The House voted on a motion to recommit the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, which would have provided military and security assistance to Ukraine, and the motion failed, allowing the bill to proceed.
The House voted down an amendment to eliminate all non-military funding for Ukraine from the supplemental appropriations bill.
The House passed H.R. 6323, the Iran Counterterrorism Act, imposing new sanctions on Iran.

The House passed a bill to rescind presidential waivers and licenses that allowed for the transfer of approximately $6 billion in blocked Iranian funds, effectively reinstating sanctions restrictions on those assets.

The bill restricts the President's authority to unilaterally terminate or waive Iran sanctions, and requires the President to report to Congress before taking such actions. Congress has 30 days (extendable to 60 days) to review the report, and can enact a joint resolution approving or disapproving the action. If Congress disapproves, the President is prohibited from taking the action. The bill als
The bill would impose sanctions on Ansarallah and foreign persons associated with them, and designate them as a foreign terrorist organization.

The bill eliminates a sunset clause in the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996, making permanent the requirement for the President to impose sanctions on certain individuals or entities engaged in specified transactions related to Iran's energy sector or Iran's efforts to acquire or develop certain weapons (such as chemical, biological, or nuclear weapons). The bill passed.

The bill passed the House of Representatives on April 16, 2024, imposing sanctions on Iran for its support of acts of international terrorism, proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and providing financial assistance to Iran.
The bill requires the President to report on funds held by certain Iranian leaders and mandates U.S. and foreign financial institutions to close those accounts, imposing sanctions on Iranian leaders.

Passed the No U.S. Financing for Iran Act, which prohibits U.S. financial institutions from transacting with Iran and bars U.S. support for IMF financial assistance to Iran, with exceptions for humanitarian goods.

Passed the Iran-China Energy Sanctions Act, which imposes secondary sanctions on Chinese financial institutions that purchase petroleum from Iran by barring U.S. financial institutions from maintaining accounts with them.

Passed the Upholding the Dayton Peace Agreement Through Sanctions Act, which imposes visa and property-blocking sanctions on foreign persons threatening the peace, stability, or territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The bill would provide supplemental security assistance to Israel; a 'Nay' vote opposes the aid.

The House passed the No Funds for Iranian Terrorism Act, which requires the President to impose property-blocking sanctions on foreign financial institutions that facilitate transactions involving specific Iranian funds transferred to Qatar.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the President from exercising waiver authority regarding sanctions on Iran under the 2012 NDAA and the Iran Freedom and Counter-Proliferation Act.
The House agreed to an amendment to H.R. 5961 prohibiting the use of federal funds to make funds available to Iran.

Passed the Hamas and Other Palestinian Terrorist Groups International Financing Prevention Act, which imposes mandatory property-blocking sanctions and bars foreign governments supporting designated terrorist groups from receiving U.S. assistance and exports.
Amendment to prohibit using funds to transfer cluster munitions to any foreign country.

The House rejected an amendment that would have prohibited the sale or transfer of cluster munitions to Ukraine.
The House voted down an amendment that would have struck a provision funding a feasibility study for a U.S. Center of Excellence in Ukraine.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited providing security assistance to Ukraine.
The House voted on a resolution directing the President to remove U.S. armed forces from Somalia under the War Powers Resolution, which failed.
The House voted on a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from Syria pursuant to the War Powers Resolution.

The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the sale of new F-16s or upgrade technology to Turkey unless the President certifies that the transfer is in the U.S. national interest and includes steps to prevent unauthorized overflights of Greece.
The House voted down an amendment to prohibit U.S. military presence in Syria without congressional approval within one year.

Passed the Isolate Russian Government Officials Act of 2022, requiring U.S. agencies to exclude Russian government officials from international financial meetings and forums until Russia ceases destabilizing activities in Ukraine.
Passed the Russia and Belarus Financial Sanctions Act of 2022, requiring U.S. financial institutions to ensure their foreign subsidiaries comply with U.S. sanctions on Russia and Belarus.

Passed the Additional Ukraine Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2022, providing $40.1 billion in emergency aid including defense equipment, economic assistance, and refugee support to Ukraine in response to Russia's invasion.

Passed the Stop Iranian Drones Act, which expands sanctions to cover the provision of unmanned combat aerial vehicles to Iran and requires the designation of Iranian entities that attack U.S. citizens with drones as foreign terrorist organizations.

Passed the Asset Seizure for Ukraine Reconstruction Act, which establishes a working group to determine legal mechanisms for seizing assets of Russian officials and recommends additional energy-related sanctions on Russia.
The House voted to suspend normal trade relations with Russia and Belarus and authorize additional visa and property-blocking sanctions in response to the war in Ukraine.
Passed a bill suspending normal trade relations with Russia and Belarus and authorizing the President to impose increased tariffs and permanent human rights sanctions.
The bill bans the importation of Russian energy products, imposing trade sanctions on Russia.
The House agreed to an amendment requiring the suspension of U.S. sustainment and maintenance support to Saudi Air Force units responsible for civilian casualties in Yemen.
The amendment terminated U.S. military logistical support, spare parts transfers, and coordination efforts for Saudi and UAE-led coalition forces conducting strikes in Yemen.
The amendment to prohibit U.S. military presence in Syria without Congressional approval within one year of enactment failed.
Passed the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act for FY2022, which included funding for foreign aid, military assistance, and international organizations.
House voted to repeal the Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002.
The House voted 204-2 to reject a motion to repeal the Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002.

On the anchor issue — aid to Israel — she is explicitly inconsistent: 4 of 6 votes anti, but she voted interventionist on a motion to recommit the Israel Security Assistance Support Act (2024-05-16) and on the Greene amendment to strike Israeli cooperative funding (2025-07-18). The framework requires a sitting member to have voted anti-interventionist on Israel aid and stayed consistent; she did not. In supporting areas she has improved: sanctions and use of force abroad became consistent in recent congresses, and war authorizations are consistently anti (5 of 5). However, military aid to other countries remains inconsistent (4 of 32 anti). She has 5 breaking anti votes total, only 2 on the anchor, and many anti votes align with her party majority (97-100%), suggesting partisan alignment more than principle. She has signed no discharge petitions against her own leadership (0 of 0 applicable). No AIPAC-tracked money appears, but the anchor failure is decisive. Under pressure, her record shows she will break on Israel aid when leadership pushes.
BG:W000187.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because she has not stayed consistent on the anchor issue of aid to Israel, voting interventionist on key Israel aid votes in 2024 and 2025 after earlier anti votes, and has zero discharge petitions against her own leadership

BG:L000593.description: Michael Ted Levin is an American politician and attorney serving as the U.S. representative for California's 49th congressional district since 2019. A member of the Democratic Party, Levin represents most of San Diego's North County, including Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, as well as a portion of southern Orange County. He is currently serving his fourth term. Levin flipped the historically Republican-held seat in 2018 after the retirement of Darrell Issa and has won four consecutive elections in the competitive district. BG:J000305.tier_writeup: Sara Jacobs (D-CA-51) has served in the House since 2021 and shows a mixed anti-interventionist record. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, she has voted both anti-interventionist (against HR 7217 in Feb 2024, against HR 8369 in May 2024, and for an amendment to prohibit funds in HR 8595 in July 2026) and interventionist (for HR 8034 in April 2024 providing military aid, and against an amendment to strike Israeli funding in HR 4016 in July 2025). This inconsistency means she has not stayed consistently anti-interventionist on Israel aid, which is the floor for reliability. She has 9 breaking anti votes across other areas and 8 party defections, but many of her anti votes align with her party majority. She has signed discharge petitions, but none that defied her own leadership. No tracked Israel lobby money appears in her donations. Her signals on use of force, war authorizations, and sanctions have become more consistently anti-interventionist recently, but the anchor failure and flip-flopping on Israel aid prevent a hard rating.
BG:J000305.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because her record on aid to Israel is inconsistent, including votes for military aid to Israel in 2024 and 2025 that break the anchor requirement.

BG:L000557.tier_screen: marked anti on the focus issue by votes or statements
BG:L000557.tier_writeup: John Larson (D-CT-1) has served since 1999 but lost his 2026 primary. On the anchor issue — aid to Israel — his record is inconsistent: only 2 of 6 votes were anti-interventionist, and his most recent votes (2025-07-18 HR 4016, 2026-07-15 HR 8595) were interventionist, so he never met the floor of voting anti and staying consistent. He has only one breaking anti vote total, and 25 of his 26 anti votes came with his own party majority, indicating partisanship rather than principle. He cosponsored the Enhanced Iran Sanctions Act (HR 1422) and voted for military aid to Ukraine and Taiwan. On supporting areas he improved — use-of-force and war-authorization votes became consistently anti — but sanctions only "became consistent" and military aid to other countries remains inconsistent (3 of 32 anti). He signed several discharge petitions, but every one had 100% Democratic signers, meaning none defied his own leadership. No TrackAIPAC money is recorded, but there is also no evidence he was targeted by the lobby. With the anchor area failed, minimal own-party defections, and no leadership defiance, he does not meet the threshold for a reliable anti-establishment ally.
BG:L000557.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he fails the anchor-area floor: his aid-to-Israel votes are inconsistent (only 2 of 6 anti, with recent votes interventionist), he has just one breaking anti vote, nearly all anti votes align with his party majority,

BG:D000216.tier_writeup: Rosa DeLauro (D-CT-3) has served in the House since 1991 and chairs the Appropriations Committee. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, she has voted interventionist four times and anti-interventionist only twice, most recently voting against an amendment to prohibit funds for Israel in July 2026 (HR 8595). Her military aid record is inconsistent: she votes anti on Saudi Arabia and Turkey but repeatedly supports aid to Ukraine and Taiwan, with only 4 anti votes out of 32. She has become consistent on sanctions (anti on Ansarallah and Iran) and on use of force abroad (12 of 15 anti), and consistently opposes war authorizations (5 of 5 anti). However, only 3 of her anti votes defy her own party, and just 2 are breaking votes; 25 of 27 anti votes align with the Democratic majority. She has signed discharge petitions but none against her own leadership. No TrackAIPAC money is recorded, though she pledged to reject AIPAC support in 2026. Her pattern shows partisan alignment, not principled anti-establishment defiance.

BG:B001257.description: Gus Michael Bilirakis is an American lawyer and politician serving as the U.S. representative for Florida's 12th congressional district since 2013. A member of the Republican Party, he first entered Congress in 2007, where he succeeded his father Michael Bilirakis, representing Florida's 9th congressional district until redistricting. His district includes much of the northern portion of the Tampa Bay area. Bilirakis previously served as the Florida state representative for the 48th district from 1998 to 2006.

BG:W000808.description: Frederica Patricia Wilson is an American politician who has been a member of the United States House of Representatives since 2011, representing Florida's 24th congressional district. Located in South Florida, Wilson's congressional district, numbered 17th during her first term, covers a large swath of eastern Miami-Dade County. The district contains most of Miami's majority-black precincts. Wilson gained national attention in 2012 for her comments on the death of Trayvon Martin. In May 2026, Wilson announced her retirement.

H. Con. Res. 89 passed, directing the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds for Ukraine Security Assistance, except for U.S. embassy security.

The Amendment sought to prohibit the Department of Defense from using taxpayer funds to cover the costs of foreign military personnel participating in bilateral or multilateral military exercises conducted with the United States unless the Secretary of Defense waives the prohibition when necessary to support a U.S. national security interest.
The House voted on a motion to recommit the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2027, which failed, allowing the bill to proceed.
The House rejected an amendment to prohibit the use of $2.1 billion in appropriated funds for Jordan, including military and health programs.
The Amendment sought to prohibit funds appropriated by the Act from being used for Israel, and accordingly reduces the Foreign Military Financing Program account by $3,300,000,000.

H. Con. Res. 108 passed by the House of Representatives on June 30, 2026, instructs the President to remove U.S. troops from hostilities in Lebanon, as per section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution. The vote failed with 187 yea, 22 nay, and 2 nay.
Passed the Ukraine Support Act to provide military and financial assistance to Ukraine.

The House passed a supplemental appropriations bill providing military and security aid to Israel.

Passed the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, providing emergency funding for military assistance, including the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative and Foreign Military Financing, as well as economic support and refugee assistance.

The House voted on a motion to recommit the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, which would have provided military and security assistance to Ukraine, and the motion failed, allowing the bill to proceed.
The House voted down an amendment to eliminate all non-military funding for Ukraine from the supplemental appropriations bill.
The House passed H.R. 6323, the Iran Counterterrorism Act, imposing new sanctions on Iran.

The House passed a bill to rescind presidential waivers and licenses that allowed for the transfer of approximately $6 billion in blocked Iranian funds, effectively reinstating sanctions restrictions on those assets.

The bill restricts the President's authority to unilaterally terminate or waive Iran sanctions, and requires the President to report to Congress before taking such actions. Congress has 30 days (extendable to 60 days) to review the report, and can enact a joint resolution approving or disapproving the action. If Congress disapproves, the President is prohibited from taking the action. The bill als
The bill would impose sanctions on Ansarallah and foreign persons associated with them, and designate them as a foreign terrorist organization.

The bill eliminates a sunset clause in the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996, making permanent the requirement for the President to impose sanctions on certain individuals or entities engaged in specified transactions related to Iran's energy sector or Iran's efforts to acquire or develop certain weapons (such as chemical, biological, or nuclear weapons). The bill passed.

The bill passed the House of Representatives on April 16, 2024, imposing sanctions on Iran for its support of acts of international terrorism, proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and providing financial assistance to Iran.
The bill requires the President to report on funds held by certain Iranian leaders and mandates U.S. and foreign financial institutions to close those accounts, imposing sanctions on Iranian leaders.

Passed the No U.S. Financing for Iran Act, which prohibits U.S. financial institutions from transacting with Iran and bars U.S. support for IMF financial assistance to Iran, with exceptions for humanitarian goods.

Passed the Iran-China Energy Sanctions Act, which imposes secondary sanctions on Chinese financial institutions that purchase petroleum from Iran by barring U.S. financial institutions from maintaining accounts with them.

Passed the Upholding the Dayton Peace Agreement Through Sanctions Act, which imposes visa and property-blocking sanctions on foreign persons threatening the peace, stability, or territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The bill would provide supplemental security assistance to Israel; a 'Nay' vote opposes the aid.

The House passed the No Funds for Iranian Terrorism Act, which requires the President to impose property-blocking sanctions on foreign financial institutions that facilitate transactions involving specific Iranian funds transferred to Qatar.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the President from exercising waiver authority regarding sanctions on Iran under the 2012 NDAA and the Iran Freedom and Counter-Proliferation Act.
The House agreed to an amendment to H.R. 5961 prohibiting the use of federal funds to make funds available to Iran.

Passed the Hamas and Other Palestinian Terrorist Groups International Financing Prevention Act, which imposes mandatory property-blocking sanctions and bars foreign governments supporting designated terrorist groups from receiving U.S. assistance and exports.
Amendment to prohibit using funds to transfer cluster munitions to any foreign country.

The House rejected an amendment that would have prohibited the sale or transfer of cluster munitions to Ukraine.
The House voted down an amendment that would have struck a provision funding a feasibility study for a U.S. Center of Excellence in Ukraine.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited providing security assistance to Ukraine.
The House voted on a resolution directing the President to remove U.S. armed forces from Somalia under the War Powers Resolution, which failed.
The House voted on a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from Syria pursuant to the War Powers Resolution.

The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the sale of new F-16s or upgrade technology to Turkey unless the President certifies that the transfer is in the U.S. national interest and includes steps to prevent unauthorized overflights of Greece.
The House voted down an amendment to prohibit U.S. military presence in Syria without congressional approval within one year.

Passed the Isolate Russian Government Officials Act of 2022, requiring U.S. agencies to exclude Russian government officials from international financial meetings and forums until Russia ceases destabilizing activities in Ukraine.
Passed the Russia and Belarus Financial Sanctions Act of 2022, requiring U.S. financial institutions to ensure their foreign subsidiaries comply with U.S. sanctions on Russia and Belarus.

Passed the Additional Ukraine Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2022, providing $40.1 billion in emergency aid including defense equipment, economic assistance, and refugee support to Ukraine in response to Russia's invasion.

Passed the Stop Iranian Drones Act, which expands sanctions to cover the provision of unmanned combat aerial vehicles to Iran and requires the designation of Iranian entities that attack U.S. citizens with drones as foreign terrorist organizations.

Passed the Asset Seizure for Ukraine Reconstruction Act, which establishes a working group to determine legal mechanisms for seizing assets of Russian officials and recommends additional energy-related sanctions on Russia.
The House voted to suspend normal trade relations with Russia and Belarus and authorize additional visa and property-blocking sanctions in response to the war in Ukraine.
Passed a bill suspending normal trade relations with Russia and Belarus and authorizing the President to impose increased tariffs and permanent human rights sanctions.
The bill bans the importation of Russian energy products, imposing trade sanctions on Russia.
The House agreed to an amendment requiring the suspension of U.S. sustainment and maintenance support to Saudi Air Force units responsible for civilian casualties in Yemen.
The amendment terminated U.S. military logistical support, spare parts transfers, and coordination efforts for Saudi and UAE-led coalition forces conducting strikes in Yemen.
The amendment to prohibit U.S. military presence in Syria without Congressional approval within one year of enactment failed.
Passed the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act for FY2022, which included funding for foreign aid, military assistance, and international organizations.

BG:D000600.description: Mario Rafael Díaz-Balart y Caballero is an American politician serving as the U.S. representative for Florida's 26th congressional district. A member of the Republican Party, he was elected in 2002, and his district includes much of northwestern Miami-Dade County, including Hialeah, and much of the northern portion of the Everglades.

BG:B000490.description: Sanford Dixon Bishop Jr. is an American lawyer and politician serving as the U.S. representative for Georgia's 2nd congressional district since 1993. He became the dean of Georgia's congressional delegation after the death of John Lewis. A member of the Blue Dog Coalition, he belongs to the moderate faction of the Democratic Party. His district is in southwestern Georgia and includes Albany, Thomasville, and most of Columbus and Macon.

BG:W000788.tier_writeup: Nikema Williams (D-GA-5) has served in the House since 2021 after leading the Georgia Democratic Party. Her record on the anchor issue — aid to Israel — is inconsistent: she cast two anti-intervention votes (against supplemental Israel aid in Feb 2024 and the Israel Security Assistance Support Act in May 2024) but also voted for a major Israel supplemental in April 2024, supported a motion to recommit that bill, and opposed an amendment to block Israeli cooperative programs in 2025. She has zero breaking anti-intervention votes on Israel aid. On supporting areas, she is consistent against war authorizations (5 of 5 anti) and has become consistent on restraining use of force (12 of 15 anti in recent Congresses), but military aid to other countries (6 of 32 anti) and sanctions (5 of 19 anti) remain inconsistent, with slips on Ukraine, Taiwan, and Iran sanctions. Only 5 of her 30 anti-intervention votes broke with her party majority; 25 aligned with it. She signed several discharge petitions but all were backed unanimously by Democrats, showing no defiance of her own leadership. No Israel-lobby money is tracked, but her party-leadership background and safe district reduce political risk. The record shows real anti-war signals on war powers and force restraint, but the anchor-area inconsistency and absence of own-party defiance on Israel aid mean she cannot be counted as reliable.
BG:W000788.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because her anchor-area record on Israel aid is inconsistent and she lacks leadership defiance.

BG:F000485.tier_writeup: Clay Fuller is a sitting Republican from Georgia who won a special election in 2026 to replace Marjorie Taylor Greene. His record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is interventionist, as he voted against an amendment to prohibit funds for Israel in H R 8595. He has voted against every resolution directing the removal of U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran, Lebanon, and other areas, aligning with 97-100% of his party. While he voted against the Ukraine Support Act and an amendment to prohibit Ukraine security assistance, these are his only anti-intervention votes. He cosponsored the United States-Israel FUTURES Act of 2026, which provides aid to Israel, and the Iran Human Rights, Internet Freedom, and Accountability Act of 2026. His voting pattern suggests he is a standard establishment Republican who occasionally opposes specific foreign aid packages but does not hold a consistent anti-interventionist principle. There is no evidence of him breaking with his party on the core issues of war authorization or use of force.
BG:F000485.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he voted for aid to Israel and failed to support any measure restraining U.S. force, while his two anti-intervention votes on Ukraine aid were inconsistent with his broader record and likely reactive.

BG:F000446.description: Randall Lee Feenstra is an American politician and businessman serving as the U.S. representative for Iowa's 4th congressional district. The district covers the state's western border and its northwestern quadrant, including Sioux City, Ames, Council Bluffs, and Marshalltown. Feenstra retired in 2026 to run for Governor of Iowa. A member of the Republican Party, Feenstra served in the Iowa Senate from the 2nd district from 2009 to 2021. He was the Sioux County treasurer from 2006 to 2008.

The House voted down an amendment to eliminate all non-military funding for Ukraine from the supplemental appropriations bill.
The House passed H.R. 6323, the Iran Counterterrorism Act, imposing new sanctions on Iran.

The House passed a bill to rescind presidential waivers and licenses that allowed for the transfer of approximately $6 billion in blocked Iranian funds, effectively reinstating sanctions restrictions on those assets.

The bill restricts the President's authority to unilaterally terminate or waive Iran sanctions, and requires the President to report to Congress before taking such actions. Congress has 30 days (extendable to 60 days) to review the report, and can enact a joint resolution approving or disapproving the action. If Congress disapproves, the President is prohibited from taking the action. The bill als
The bill would impose sanctions on Ansarallah and foreign persons associated with them, and designate them as a foreign terrorist organization.

The bill eliminates a sunset clause in the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996, making permanent the requirement for the President to impose sanctions on certain individuals or entities engaged in specified transactions related to Iran's energy sector or Iran's efforts to acquire or develop certain weapons (such as chemical, biological, or nuclear weapons). The bill passed.

The bill passed the House of Representatives on April 16, 2024, imposing sanctions on Iran for its support of acts of international terrorism, proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and providing financial assistance to Iran.
The bill requires the President to report on funds held by certain Iranian leaders and mandates U.S. and foreign financial institutions to close those accounts, imposing sanctions on Iranian leaders.

Passed the No U.S. Financing for Iran Act, which prohibits U.S. financial institutions from transacting with Iran and bars U.S. support for IMF financial assistance to Iran, with exceptions for humanitarian goods.

Passed the Iran-China Energy Sanctions Act, which imposes secondary sanctions on Chinese financial institutions that purchase petroleum from Iran by barring U.S. financial institutions from maintaining accounts with them.
The bill would provide supplemental security assistance to Israel; a 'Nay' vote opposes the aid.

The House passed the No Funds for Iranian Terrorism Act, which requires the President to impose property-blocking sanctions on foreign financial institutions that facilitate transactions involving specific Iranian funds transferred to Qatar.

The House agreed to an amendment to H.R. 5961 prohibiting the use of federal funds to make funds available to Iran.

The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the sale of new F-16s or upgrade technology to Turkey unless the President certifies that the transfer is in the U.S. national interest and includes steps to prevent unauthorized overflights of Greece.
The House voted down an amendment to prohibit U.S. military presence in Syria without congressional approval within one year.

Passed the Isolate Russian Government Officials Act of 2022, requiring U.S. agencies to exclude Russian government officials from international financial meetings and forums until Russia ceases destabilizing activities in Ukraine.
Passed the Russia and Belarus Financial Sanctions Act of 2022, requiring U.S. financial institutions to ensure their foreign subsidiaries comply with U.S. sanctions on Russia and Belarus.

Passed the Additional Ukraine Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2022, providing $40.1 billion in emergency aid including defense equipment, economic assistance, and refugee support to Ukraine in response to Russia's invasion.

Passed the Stop Iranian Drones Act, which expands sanctions to cover the provision of unmanned combat aerial vehicles to Iran and requires the designation of Iranian entities that attack U.S. citizens with drones as foreign terrorist organizations.

Passed the Asset Seizure for Ukraine Reconstruction Act, which establishes a working group to determine legal mechanisms for seizing assets of Russian officials and recommends additional energy-related sanctions on Russia.
The House voted to suspend normal trade relations with Russia and Belarus and authorize additional visa and property-blocking sanctions in response to the war in Ukraine.
Passed a bill suspending normal trade relations with Russia and Belarus and authorizing the President to impose increased tariffs and permanent human rights sanctions.
The bill bans the importation of Russian energy products, imposing trade sanctions on Russia.
The amendment terminated U.S. military logistical support, spare parts transfers, and coordination efforts for Saudi and UAE-led coalition forces conducting strikes in Yemen.
The amendment to prohibit U.S. military presence in Syria without Congressional approval within one year of enactment failed.
Passed the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act for FY2022, which included funding for foreign aid, military assistance, and international organizations.
House voted to repeal the Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002.
The House voted 204-2 to reject a motion to repeal the Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002.

BG:Q000023.tier_writeup: Mike Quigley (D-IL5) has served in the House since 2009. His record on the anchor issue — aid to Israel — is inconsistent: he cast three anti votes and three interventionist votes across six roll calls, with no sustained turn toward the anti-interventionist side. On supporting areas he is mixed: military aid to other countries (3 of 31 anti, consistent only on Saudi Arabia and Turkey), sanctions (2 of 19 anti, consistent only on Ansarallah), use of force abroad (11 of 15 anti, recently consistent), and war authorizations (5 of 5 anti). Only two of his anti-intervention votes broke with his own party; 22 came with the Democratic majority, indicating partisanship rather than principle. He has signed multiple discharge petitions, but every one had 100% Democratic signers, showing no defiance of his own leadership. No TrackAIPAC or war-profiteer money is recorded, but neither is there evidence of being targeted by that lobby. The record shows a conventional establishment Democrat who votes anti-intervention when his party does, not when it costs him.
BG:Q000023.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because his anchor-area record on aid to Israel is inconsistent (3 of 6 anti), he has only two career party defections on anti-intervention votes, and he has never signed a discharge petition that defied his own leadership.

BG:D000096.tier_writeup: Danny Davis (D-IL-7) is a long-serving incumbent who is retiring after the 2026 primary. His record on the anchor issue — aid to Israel — is inconsistent: only 2 of 4 votes were anti-interventionist, and both aligned with most Democrats (78% and 48% same), showing no principled break with party leadership. On military aid to other countries he voted anti just 5 of 31 times, frequently supporting packages for Ukraine, Taiwan and Lebanon. Sanctions and use-of-force votes became more anti-interventionist in recent congresses, but nearly all occurred with overwhelming Democratic majorities (97–100% same), indicating partisanship rather than principle. War authorization votes were consistently anti but again with 98–99% of his party. He has five total party defections to the anti side, yet none on the anchor issue and none paired with leadership defiance. He signed zero discharge petitions against his own leadership. No TrackAIPAC money is recorded, but AIPAC-aligned spending targets his district. Because the anchor area never held and there is no evidence of costly principle, he falls below the floor for reliability.
BG:D000096.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because the anchor area (aid to Israel) is inconsistent and the member has no breaking anti-interventionist vote against their own leadership on that issue, nor any discharge petition defiance.

BG:S001145.tier_writeup: Jan Schakowsky (D-IL9) is a long-serving progressive Democrat who is retiring after the 2026 primary. Her record shows genuine anti-interventionist votes on use of force abroad (14 of 15 anti) and war authorizations (5 of 5 anti), and she has become consistent on sanctions (6 of 19 anti, with recent consistency on Iran, Palestine, and Ansarallah). However, the anchor area — aid to Israel — is inconsistent: only 3 of 6 votes anti, with interventionist votes in 2024 and 2025 (HR 8034, HR 4016). Military aid to other countries is also inconsistent (7 of 31 anti) and she voted interventionist on Ukraine, Taiwan, and Lebanon amendments in 2025-2026. She has 9 party defections to anti, but most occurred early (2023-2024); recent votes align with her party majority (97-100% same). She signed several discharge petitions, but all had 100% Democratic signers, showing no leadership defiance. She sponsored a resolution supporting Israeli democracy (HCONRES 61). No TrackAIPAC money is recorded, but she has not been targeted by the lobby either. The anchor-area failure and lack of sustained leadership defiance mean she cannot be counted as reliable.
BG:S001145.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because her anchor-area record on aid to Israel is inconsistent and she has not defied leadership on discharge petitions, leaving her anti-intervention signals real but unreliable.

The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds for Ukraine Security Assistance, except for U.S. embassy security.

The bill would impose sanctions on Ansarallah and foreign persons associated with them, and designate them as a foreign terrorist organization.

Passed the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, providing emergency funding for military assistance, including the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative and Foreign Military Financing, as well as economic support and refugee assistance.

The House voted on a motion to recommit the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, which would have provided military and security assistance to Ukraine, and the motion failed, allowing the bill to proceed.
The House voted down an amendment to eliminate all non-military funding for Ukraine from the supplemental appropriations bill.
The House passed H.R. 6323, the Iran Counterterrorism Act, imposing new sanctions on Iran.

The House passed a bill to rescind presidential waivers and licenses that allowed for the transfer of approximately $6 billion in blocked Iranian funds, effectively reinstating sanctions restrictions on those assets.

The bill restricts the President's authority to unilaterally terminate or waive Iran sanctions, and requires the President to report to Congress before taking such actions. Congress has 30 days (extendable to 60 days) to review the report, and can enact a joint resolution approving or disapproving the action. If Congress disapproves, the President is prohibited from taking the action. The bill als
The bill would impose sanctions on Ansarallah and foreign persons associated with them, and designate them as a foreign terrorist organization.

The bill eliminates a sunset clause in the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996, making permanent the requirement for the President to impose sanctions on certain individuals or entities engaged in specified transactions related to Iran's energy sector or Iran's efforts to acquire or develop certain weapons (such as chemical, biological, or nuclear weapons). The bill passed.

The bill passed the House of Representatives on April 16, 2024, imposing sanctions on Iran for its support of acts of international terrorism, proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and providing financial assistance to Iran.
The bill requires the President to report on funds held by certain Iranian leaders and mandates U.S. and foreign financial institutions to close those accounts, imposing sanctions on Iranian leaders.

Passed the No U.S. Financing for Iran Act, which prohibits U.S. financial institutions from transacting with Iran and bars U.S. support for IMF financial assistance to Iran, with exceptions for humanitarian goods.

Passed the Iran-China Energy Sanctions Act, which imposes secondary sanctions on Chinese financial institutions that purchase petroleum from Iran by barring U.S. financial institutions from maintaining accounts with them.

Passed the Upholding the Dayton Peace Agreement Through Sanctions Act, which imposes visa and property-blocking sanctions on foreign persons threatening the peace, stability, or territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The bill would provide supplemental security assistance to Israel; a 'Nay' vote opposes the aid.

The House passed the No Funds for Iranian Terrorism Act, which requires the President to impose property-blocking sanctions on foreign financial institutions that facilitate transactions involving specific Iranian funds transferred to Qatar.

The House agreed to an amendment to H.R. 5961 prohibiting the use of federal funds to make funds available to Iran.

Passed the Isolate Russian Government Officials Act of 2022, requiring U.S. agencies to exclude Russian government officials from international financial meetings and forums until Russia ceases destabilizing activities in Ukraine.
Passed the Russia and Belarus Financial Sanctions Act of 2022, requiring U.S. financial institutions to ensure their foreign subsidiaries comply with U.S. sanctions on Russia and Belarus.

Passed the Additional Ukraine Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2022, providing $40.1 billion in emergency aid including defense equipment, economic assistance, and refugee support to Ukraine in response to Russia's invasion.

Passed the Stop Iranian Drones Act, which expands sanctions to cover the provision of unmanned combat aerial vehicles to Iran and requires the designation of Iranian entities that attack U.S. citizens with drones as foreign terrorist organizations.

Passed the Asset Seizure for Ukraine Reconstruction Act, which establishes a working group to determine legal mechanisms for seizing assets of Russian officials and recommends additional energy-related sanctions on Russia.
The House voted to suspend normal trade relations with Russia and Belarus and authorize additional visa and property-blocking sanctions in response to the war in Ukraine.
Passed a bill suspending normal trade relations with Russia and Belarus and authorizing the President to impose increased tariffs and permanent human rights sanctions.
The bill bans the importation of Russian energy products, imposing trade sanctions on Russia.
The House agreed to an amendment requiring the suspension of U.S. sustainment and maintenance support to Saudi Air Force units responsible for civilian casualties in Yemen.
The amendment terminated U.S. military logistical support, spare parts transfers, and coordination efforts for Saudi and UAE-led coalition forces conducting strikes in Yemen.
The amendment to prohibit U.S. military presence in Syria without Congressional approval within one year of enactment failed.

A member of the Republican Party, he has served in Congress since 2016, during the 114th United States Congress. He previously served in the Kentucky House of Representatives and also served as the agriculture commissioner of Kentucky.

BG:M001184.tier_writeup: Thomas Massie is a sitting Republican representative from Kentucky who has served since 2012 and is widely recognized for his libertarian and anti-interventionist stance. His voting record is exceptionally consistent, with 71 of 72 focus votes cast on the anti-interventionist side, including 6 of 6 votes against aid to the State of Israel. He has consistently voted against military aid to countries such as Ukraine, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Taiwan, as well as against sanctions on Russia, Iran, and China. Massie has repeatedly broken with his own party leadership, casting 68 breaking anti-interventionist votes, often when over 90% of his Republican colleagues voted the other way. He signed multiple discharge petitions to bypass his own party's leadership on war powers and foreign policy issues. Financially, he received zero dollars from the Israel lobby (TrackAIPAC) but was targeted by $3.9 million in outside spending from groups like the United Democracy Project, indicating he is viewed as a threat by establishment interests. His record has held firm through the 117th, 118th, and 119th Congresses, showing no signs of political posturing or inconsistency. Although he lost his 2026 primary to a Trump-endorsed candidate, his legislative record remains a reliable indicator of his principles.

BG:H001077.description: Glen Clay Higgins is an American politician and reserve law enforcement officer from the state of Louisiana. A Republican, Higgins is the U.S. representative for Louisiana's 3rd congressional district. The district, which contains much of the territory once represented by former governor Edwin Edwards and former U.S. senator John Breaux, is in the southwestern corner of the state and includes Lafayette, Lake Charles, and New Iberia. Higgins won the runoff election on December 10, 2016, defeating fellow Republican Scott Angelle.

BG:N000015.description: Richard Edmund Neal is an American politician serving as the U.S. representative for Massachusetts's 1st congressional district since 1989. The district, numbered as the 2nd district from 1989 to 2013, includes Springfield, West Springfield, Pittsfield, Holyoke, Agawam, Chicopee, and Westfield. A member of the Democratic Party, Neal has been the dean of Massachusetts's delegation to the United States House of Representatives since 2013, and is dean of the New England House delegations.

BG:T000482.description: Lori Ann Trahan is an American businesswoman and politician serving as the U.S. representative for Massachusetts's 3rd congressional district since 2019. The district covers Boston's northwestern suburbs, and includes Lowell, Lawrence, Concord, and Trahan's hometown, Westford. A Democrat, she formerly served as chief of staff to Representative Marty Meehan in Massachusetts's 5th congressional district.
